newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's Krupp confirms hostile bid for rival Thyssen.
newsitem.headline: Germany's Krupp confirms hostile bid for rival Thyssen.

text.p: German industry giant Krupp confirmed Tuesday that it planned to launch a hostile takeover bid for rival Thyssen AG, a move that would create one of the world's largest steel and engineering conglomerates.

The merger would form a European powerhouse with annual revenues of some 63 billion marks ($37.3 billion) that would be big enough to challenge its larger European competitors -- Usinor Sacilor of France and British Steel Plc -- and could spark further industry consolidation.

Krupp, formally known as Fried. Krupp AG Hoesch-Krupp, said it would offer Thyssen shareholders 435 marks a share, a 25 percent premium on Monday's closing share price, in a rare hostile takeover bid.
The announcement sparked an angry response from Thyssen, which was caught off guard by the unexpected grab for control of its capital. It said it would seek to ward off Krupp.
"We will seek to effectively fend off this hostile takeover with partners from government and industry," Thyssen said in a statement.
The news also prompted steel workers fearing massive lay-offs to stage angry protests throughout the Ruhr Valley, Germany's industrial heartland.

Krupp Chief Executive Gerhard Cromme -- dubbed the "job killer" after his spectacular 1991 takeover of Hoesch that resulted in 20,000 job cuts -- was shouted down by workers at Krupp offices as he tried to explain the takeover.
Speaking behind a wall of riot shields under a din of shouting workers, Cromme dismissed Thyssen's allegations that a takeover would cost "tens of thousands" of jobs.

"The numbers that are making the rounds are nothing but panic-mongering," he said, adding that it made sense in the interest of retaining competitive jobs in the Ruhr Valley to forge a union of Germany's top two steel companies.
Cromme gave no details of the company's plans, although a Krupp spokesman said that the Essen-based industrial titan was "fairly certain" the bid would succeed.

About 1,000 Thyssen steel workers protested at the Krupp headquarters. Some attempted to charge the building while others threw eggs and oranges at the Krupp chairman shouting "Where is the (jobs) killer?" and "Come out, Cromme!"
In Dortmund, where Krupp's steel activities are based at the former Hoesch Stahl plant, its workers joined protests, fearing another round of job losses.
"Hoesch used to have three steel mills," said one woman wearing blue steel worker's coveralls. "Two of them are now closed and what are young people supposed to do?"

Aside from the human cost in lost jobs -- Germany's jobless rate is the worst since 1933 -- and massive shifting of social and economic structures in the country's industrial heartland, the merger makes economic sense, analysts said.

Industry analysts welcomed Krupp's move on its larger rival, saying a takeover would help consolidate the German steel industry, still ailing from chronic over capacity, although they wondered how Krupp would finance the deal.
"It looks to me like a classic case where the victim gets bid up, but the value of the buyer gets called into question," said Terence Sinclair, analyst at Salomon Brothers in London.

The takeover could also face political hurdles from government officials fearing another round of explosive protests just days after thousands of miners marched on Bonn, blocking streets and disrupting government business to protest cuts in subsidies to the coal industry.

The European Commission said it had not been notified by Germany's Federal Cartel Office of a Krupp-Thyssen merger, but European Union sources said a merger of the two steel giants would surely be reviewed by the EU.
The takeover attempt marks the second time in six years that Cromme, a Harvard Business School graduate, has shunned German aversions to hostile takeovers.
Usually, most mergers in Germany are carefully orchestrated by the bankers who sit on the boards of most German blue chip firms.
The mood was almost identical that seen during Krupp's 1991 surprise takeover of Hoesch AG.
Following the bombshell announcement that Krupp was poised to seize control of Hoesch, management and workers vowed to fight to retain their independence but it was all in vain.
Cromme had secretly amassed a sizeable stake in his rival and convinced a majority of the remaining shareholders to back the merger.

Contrary to analysts' expectations, Krupp said it would make a cash offer that would be secured by Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, the investment arm of Deutsche Bank AG, Dresdner Bank, U.S. investment bank Goldman Sachs and other unidentified institutions.
Krupp explained the move by saying that as the world economy becomes more intertwined it is crucial for companies to cut costs in production, logistics and distribution.

"That's why it is indispensable to achieve sufficient size in business areas in accordance with global standards. Only under these conditions do German companies have the chance to survive in interational competition," the company said.
Krupp added that 70 percent of the two firms' businesses were complementary.
